headline: From Work Orders to Integrated FM: What Saudi FM & Clean Showed
deck: The hall covering cleaning and facilities management spent four days talking about asset data, bundled contracts and energy.
excerpt: Saudi FM & Clean at Big 5 Construct Saudi was dominated by integrated contracts, work-order systems and energy management rather than manpower and cleaning. Al-Futtaim Engineering took the Impact Trail operational sustainability award for an integrated FM solution.
content:
Saudi FM & Clean is the part of Big 5 Construct Saudi that describes what happens after everything else in the venue has been installed, and it has outgrown the description implied by its name. The hall at Riyadh Front covered facilities management, cleaning, hygiene and waste, but the commercial conversation running through it was about asset data, contract structure and energy.

The clearest signal came from the awards. Al-Futtaim Engineering Company took the Big 5 Impact Trail prize for operational sustainability, given for an integrated facilities management solution rather than for a product. That framing matters: the thing being recognised was the ability to run hard services, soft services and energy management as one accountable scope.

The corporate moves behind it point the same way. Al-Futtaim Contracting has brought together Al-Futtaim Facilities Management with the fire and life safety division of Al-Futtaim Engineering to launch integrated FM and fire and life safety operations in the Kingdom, which bundles a compliance discipline into a maintenance contract. Fire and life safety is regulated under the Saudi Building Code's SBC 801 requirements, and since the 2024 edition became mandatory in June 2025 the consequences of a failure have moved from a commercial dispute to a permitting one.

Underneath the service model sits a market shifting from in-house to contracted delivery. Mordor Intelligence puts the outsourced share of Saudi facility management at close to 60% and growing at around 8% a year, and published estimates of the market's total size vary widely enough that the structural point is more reliable than the headline number. What outsourcing does is force measurement: an in-house team can run on institutional memory, but a client paying a contractor has to be able to verify what was done, when, and to what standard.

That is why work-order platforms, asset registers and condition data drew the attention they did. The questions FM teams asked of software vendors were narrow and practical. Does an alert become a work order in the system we already run. Who dispatches. What proportion of alarms are false. How does a technician close a job without a laptop. Vendors who answered in terms of dashboards rather than dispatch found the conversations short.

Energy is the largest controllable line in almost every Saudi operating budget, because cooling dominates building consumption for much of the year. The scale involved is easy to underestimate: the Information Technology and Communications Complex in Riyadh, developed across more than 800,000 square metres with four twenty-storey towers, operates its own district cooling plant rated above 35,000 tons of refrigeration. Optimising plant on that scale is not a facilities task in the traditional sense; it is utility operation, and it requires people who can read a control strategy.

Coordination between design, installation and operation was the theme the show's conference programme raised directly, with sessions on improving the relationship between HVACR design, installation and facilities management. It is the correct problem to raise. A large share of the energy waste in Gulf buildings is created at handover, when a system commissioned to one intent is transferred to a team that never received the intent.

Cleaning, hygiene and waste have not disappeared from the market, and they remain the largest employer within it. But they are increasingly bought as part of a bundled contract rather than as the contract itself, which changes who the client is negotiating with and what they are negotiating about.

The constraint everybody named was staffing. Condition monitoring, building management systems and analytics all assume a technician who can interpret an alarm and a supervisor who can hold a subcontractor to a response time, and those people are being competed for by the construction programme that is creating the assets in the first place. BrentDesk has argued that the larger Saudi construction opportunity may begin after handover. The hall at Riyadh Front suggested the industry agrees, and has not yet solved the labour question that comes with it.
